title: Evaluation Methodology
scopeHtml: Scope: Datasets, graders, LLM-as-judge, metrics, regression and online evaluation.

notes.title: Why evals come first
notes.html:
Definition. An eval is a fixed collection of test cases with expected behaviour and a grader that turns model outputs into scores. It makes quality measurable and comparable across prompts, models, retrieval settings and code changes.

Why LLM systems need them more than normal software. Outputs are non-deterministic and open-ended; "it looks fine on my five examples" hides failures; changes (prompt tweak, model update) have non-obvious side effects; stakeholders need evidence; and without an eval you cannot tell whether an optimization (cheaper model, shorter prompt) hurt quality.

Eval-driven development loop.

  1. Define success criteria (specific, gradable).
  2. Build the eval set and graders before the feature.
  3. Baseline simple solution → measure.
  4. Change one thing → measure → keep or revert.
  5. Gate releases on the eval; monitor in production; feed failures back.

Expectations. The first score is often poor (2 to 4 out of 10 is normal); what matters is a trend of improvement and understanding failure categories.

Real life. A thermometer: it doesn't cure the patient but tells you whether treatment works.

Interview angle. "How do you know your prompt change is an improvement?" → eval with a representative set, paired comparison, regression check.

notes.title: Datasets
notes.html:
Sources.

  • Production samples (anonymized): best match to reality; sample uniformly and oversample failures/edge cases.
  • Expert-authored cases for critical policies, compliance rules, rare but costly scenarios.
  • Synthetic generation: LLM-written variants and adversarial cases; validate quality and diversity; tends to be easier than real traffic.
  • Public benchmarks for sanity checks and comparison, not as the primary measure.
  • Red-team and adversarial sets: jailbreaks, injections, edge inputs.

Composition checklist. Common cases (weighted by frequency), hard/long-tail cases, ambiguous requests, unanswerable/out-of-scope, multi-turn conversations, multiple languages/locales, different user personas, format stress (long, short, messy, empty), safety-sensitive prompts, "should refuse/escalate" and "should not refuse" pairs.

Labelling. Expected output or rubric per case; reference answers where a single correct answer exists; properties to check otherwise (must include X, must not include Y, ≤ N words); metadata tags (category, difficulty, language) for slicing.

Size. 50 to 200 for early development; 500 to 2,000 for mature features; more for fine-grained slices. Statistical power matters: with 100 cases a 5-point difference is often noise.

Hygiene. Version the dataset; keep a frozen test split that isn't used for prompt tuning; avoid duplicates; remove leaked test items from prompts/few-shot examples; refresh with new failures regularly.

Real life. A driving test that includes rain, night and roundabouts, not only an empty road.

notes.title: Graders
notes.html:
Choosing a grader by output type.

Output Grader Strength Weakness
Single label/number Exact match / normalized match cheap, deterministic fails valid paraphrases
Structured/code Code-graded (schema valid, parses, unit tests pass, SQL result equals) objective, cheap doesn't judge quality beyond rules
Short free text with known facts Fact/keyword/semantic match, regex, embedding similarity cheap brittle or shallow
Open-ended quality LLM-as-judge with rubric scalable, handles nuance noisy, biased, costs money
High-stakes / subjective Human review gold standard slow, expensive, also inconsistent

Layer them. Cheap deterministic checks on every run (format, forbidden content, length), LLM judge for quality on every release, humans for periodic calibration and sensitive slices.

Rubric design. Specific criteria with anchored scales (what a 1, 3, 5 looks like), one criterion per question (correctness, completeness, tone, safety), pass/fail per criterion rather than a vague 1 to 10, and instructions to cite evidence.

Real life. Multiple choice is auto-marked; a coding test is run against hidden tests; an essay needs a calibrated examiner.

notes.title: LLM-as-judge done right
notes.html:
Setup. A judge model receives the task, the response(s), optional reference and a rubric, and outputs structured scores with brief reasoning.

Modes.

  • Pointwise (score one response): simple, but scores drift and compress.
  • Pairwise (which is better, A or B): more reliable for relative comparisons; run both orders to cancel position bias.
  • Reference-based: compare to a gold answer (checks correctness).
  • Reference-free: judge against the rubric/context (e.g. faithfulness to retrieved documents).
  • Multi-judge / jury: several models or prompts, aggregate (reduces variance and self-preference).

Known biases and mitigations.

  • Position bias → randomize/swap order.
  • Verbosity bias (prefers longer) → control length or instruct to ignore length; include length-matched cases.
  • Self-preference (favours its own family's style) → use a different judge model family.
  • Sycophancy to the author's claims; leniency (scores cluster high) → anchored rubrics, harder negative examples.
  • Prompt sensitivity → test judge prompt variants.

Calibration protocol.

  1. Collect 50 to 200 outputs labelled by humans (two annotators, measure agreement).
  2. Run the judge; compute agreement (accuracy, Cohen's κ, Spearman for scores) and per-class precision/recall.
  3. Inspect disagreements, refine rubric/prompt, repeat.
  4. Track judge drift when the judge model changes; re-calibrate.
  5. Keep humans in the loop on a sample every cycle.

Cost control. Cheaper judge for screening, stronger judge for ambiguous cases; cache; judge only changed outputs.

Real life. Training the judges at a competition so scores are consistent, and swapping judges to catch favouritism.

notes.title: Metrics and statistics
notes.html:
Choose metrics tied to the product.

  • Classification: accuracy, precision/recall/F1 per class, confusion matrix, cost-weighted error.
  • Generation/QA: correctness, faithfulness/groundedness, completeness, relevance, format validity, citation accuracy.
  • Code: pass@k (at least one of k samples passes), unit-test pass rate.
  • Retrieval: recall@k, MRR, nDCG.
  • Agents: task success, steps, cost, safety violations, pass^k (reliability).
  • Operational: latency percentiles, cost per request, refusal rate, escalation rate, error rate.
  • Safety: attack success rate, harmful output rate, over-refusal rate.

Statistics.

  • Report confidence intervals (bootstrap or Wilson for proportions).
  • Use paired comparisons (same cases for A and B; McNemar or paired bootstrap) — far more sensitive than unpaired.
  • Run multiple samples per case for stochastic systems; separate prompt effect from sampling noise.
  • Beware multiple comparisons (many variants → some win by chance).
  • Report by slice (language, category, difficulty) to uncover hidden regressions; don't rely on a single average.
  • Effect size and practical significance, not only p-values.

Real life. One lucky free throw doesn't make a great shooter.

notes.title: Offline, online and regression testing
notes.html:
Offline evals. Run on fixed datasets before release: development iteration, CI gating, model comparison, red-team suites. Fast and repeatable, but only as representative as the dataset.

Online evaluation.

  • Shadow mode: new version runs on live traffic without user exposure; compare outputs/metrics.
  • Canary release to 1 to 5%.
  • A/B tests on business metrics: resolution rate, task completion, retention, CSAT, revenue; guardrail metrics (latency, cost, safety).
  • Implicit feedback: edits, regenerations, abandonment, escalation, copy actions.
  • Explicit feedback: thumbs, ratings, comments; sampled human review.
  • Production monitoring with automatic graders on sampled traffic to detect drift.

Regression testing. Maintain a suite of previously failing cases and critical behaviours; run in CI on every change of prompt, model version, retrieval config, tools; pin model versions; re-run before provider upgrades; alert on metric drops beyond noise thresholds.

Closed loop. Production failures → triage → add to eval set → fix → verify → deploy.

Real life. Lab tests first, then a pilot with a small group, then full rollout, then ongoing audits.

notes.title: Common eval pitfalls
notes.html:
1. Contamination: test items in prompts, few-shot examples, fine-tuning data, or the model's training set.
  2. Overfitting to the eval: iterating prompts against the same cases until they memorize quirks; keep a frozen test split.
  3. Unrepresentative data: only easy/clean inputs; missing languages and edge cases.
  4. Uncalibrated judges: trusting scores without human agreement checks.
  5. Ignoring variance: single-run comparisons of stochastic systems.
  6. Metric mismatch: optimizing BLEU/ROUGE or length when users care about correctness.
  7. Goodhart effects: the measure becomes the target and stops reflecting quality.
  8. Averaging away failures: a catastrophic safety failure hidden in a high mean.
  9. Eval staleness: product and users change; eval doesn't.
  10. Not reading outputs: numbers hide failure modes; review samples regularly.

Real life. Teaching to the test.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
Why evals. Quality must be measurable in a non-deterministic system; write the eval before the feature; iterate with one change at a time; gate releases.

Datasets. Mix production samples, expert cases, synthetic and adversarial; include hard, ambiguous, unanswerable, multilingual and multi-turn cases; label with rubrics/properties and tags; 50 to 200 to start, more for maturity; keep a frozen test split; refresh from failures.

Graders. Exact match (single labels), code checks (structure, tests), semantic/fact matching, LLM-judge (open-ended), humans (gold/high-stakes). Layer them by cost and frequency.

LLM judge. Anchored rubrics, pairwise with order swapping, reference-based when possible, juries, different-family judges; mitigate position, verbosity and self-preference biases; calibrate against human labels (κ, accuracy) and monitor drift.

Metrics/stats. Choose product-aligned metrics, report confidence intervals, use paired tests, slice results, run multiple samples, mind multiple comparisons and practical significance.

Offline + online. CI regression suites; shadow, canary and A/B in production with guardrail metrics; feedback loops; pin model versions.

Pitfalls. Contamination, overfitting, unrepresentative data, uncalibrated judges, variance, Goodhart, averaging away failures, staleness.

Interview one-liners.

  • "No eval, no claim of improvement."
  • "Calibrate the judge against humans before trusting a single number."
  • "Paired comparisons and slices find regressions that averages hide."
  • "Every incident becomes a test case."
